NHTSA Reports US Traffic Fatalities Dropped 2.5 Percent in H1 2026
26 photos
Photo: IIHS on YouTube
The number of US motor vehicle crash fatalities has reportedly fallen by 2.5 percent in the first six months of 2026, even as American motorists drove 0.8 percent more miles than a year earlier. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, no fewer than 16,750 deaths were recorded between January and June of this year as opposed to 17,175 during the same period in 2025.
Looking at the raw data more closely, we can see that said 2.5 percent improvement was heavily concentrated in the first quarter. The second delivered almost no year-over-year reduction. Looking at the bigger picture, 425 fewer deaths in the span of six months isn't the flex certain people think it is. Based on these figures, the fatality rate fell to 1.02 deaths per 100 million vehicle miles traveled.
That is the real flex here, representing the second-lowest H1 figure in the agency's historical comparison. During the first half of 2014, the NHTSA reported a record 1.01 deaths per 100 million miles. Between January and March, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that 7,715 peeps died in motor vehicle crashes on US roads, a 5 percent decrease from Q1 2025.
The estimated toll reached 9,035 in the second quarter compared with 9,055 a year earlier. When it comes to monthly fatalities, May and June went in the opposite direction of the first four months. NHTSA estimates increases of 1.5 and 3 percent, respectively, compared with last year's corresponding months.
If we analyze the data through monthly breakdowns, the most sensible among us would not treat the decline as a consistently improving trend. The second-quarter numbers suggest that considerable momentum was lost as the year progressed and the weather got warmer. Going down the rabbit hole, state-level data shows something else.
Photo: IIHS on YouTube Per the NHTSA, 35 states and Puerto Rico experienced fewer traffic fatalities during the first half of 2026. If you ask me, I can easily understand Puerto Rico's evolution in this regard after Bad Bunny made everyone love dancing again. Jokes aside, the remaining 15 states and the District of Columbia are projected to have recorded increases.
Hawaii posted the largest decrease among the states, falling 32.4 percent from 68 to 46. West Virginia followed with a 27.8 percent reduction, while Illinois saw its projected fatalities decline 20.4 percent. North Dakota recorded a 25 percent increase, while Delaware and DC increased 28.3 and 128.6 percent. Bear in mind that small underlying numbers can make percentage comparisons sensitive to individual cases.
Texas fatalities remained almost unchanged at 1,851, and California's estimate increased to 1,825 in the analyzed period. Eight of the NHTSA's ten administrative regions are projected to have recorded declines in both fatalities and the fatality rate per 100 million miles, The other two regions are listed with estimated increases of 4 and 3 percent, respectively.
Under the P2SS action plan, the NHTSA will strengthen cooperation with police deps to identify dangerous driving and stop motorists from engaging in risky or illegal behavior. The NHTSA also highlighted increased support for prehospital blood transfusion programs, namely programs allowing medical personnel to administer blood to severely injured crash victims before reaching a hospital.
Research shows that prehospital transfusions may reduce mortality among patients suffering from severe bleeding by 37 percent. While not a 37 percent reduction in overall traffic fatalities, a greater chance of survival among a specific group of seriously injured patients is an improvement all of us can get behind.
